title: Hyperspatial Sampling: Circumventing Free-Energy Barriers via Replica Exchange with Extra Dimensions
authors: Henrik Christiansen, Matheus Ferraz, Takashi Maruyama, Francesco Alesiani
abstract: Simulating systems with rugged free-energy landscapes remains a central challenge in computational physics and chemistry. We introduce hyperspatial replica exchange (HS-REX), an enhanced sampling method in which the physical system is artificially extended by additional spatial dimensions. In higher dimensions, free-energy barriers can be circumvented through paths that are geometrically inaccessible in the original space. Restricting the penalty to only solute atoms dramatically reduces the number of replicas required for solvated systems compared to standard temperature replica exchange, a feature especially relevant for biological applications. As proof of concept, we demonstrate the method on a double-well model system and on alanine dipeptide in explicit water as benchmark system. In the latter case, HS-REX achieves enhanced conformational sampling of not only the slow backbone dihedral angles, but also both chiral configurations of the molecule, which are sterically inaccessible to standard sampling in three dimensions. This demonstrates enhanced ergodic sampling over conventional temperature replica exchange.
summary: This paper introduces Hyperspatial Replica Exchange (HS-REX), an advanced enhanced sampling technique that artificially increases the dimensionality of a physical system. By utilizing extra dimensions, HS-REX allows simulations to bypass high free-energy barriers inaccessible in the original space. This method is shown to efficiently sample complex conformational changes in biomolecules like alanine dipeptide, outperforming conventional temperature replica exchange.
main_problem: The central challenge is simulating physical systems trapped in rugged free-energy landscapes due to high energy barriers between metastable states.
main_result: Hyperspatial Replica Exchange (HS-REX) successfully circumvents these barriers by artificially extending the system into higher dimensions, achieving enhanced ergodic sampling compared to standard methods.
method: The method extends the physical Hamiltonian into extra spatial dimensions and uses a replica exchange framework where exchanges occur based on varying harmonic penalties in these added dimensions.
model_or_system: Benchmark systems include a double-well model and alanine dipeptide simulated in explicit water. The formalism involves extending the Hamiltonian to $D = d + d_+$ dimensions with a quadratic penalty term applied selectively to solute atoms.
key_observables: Enhanced conformational sampling, successful crossing of energy barriers (e.g., L/D chirality inversion), and significantly reduced round-trip simulation times compared to Parallel Tempering (PT).
important_parameters: The harmonic penalty strength ($\mu$) is varied across replicas; the method's efficiency depends on maintaining appropriate acceptance rates.
main_assumptions: The technique assumes that the added dimensions define a fast subsystem suitable for exact propagation methods, and the penalty is applied only to solute atoms to maintain physical relevance in solvated systems.
figures_summary: Figures compare free-energy surfaces ($\Delta F$) showing enhanced exploration via HS-REX versus trapping in PT. Other figures compare acceptance rates and round-trip time distributions, demonstrating superior mixing for HS-REX.
paper_structure: The paper introduces the concept of hyperspatial extension to overcome barriers, validates it on a simple double-well model, and then applies it rigorously to biomolecular systems like alanine dipeptide in water, comparing performance metrics (acceptance rates, time scales) against established methods like PT.
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the concept of mapping complex dynamics onto higher-dimensional spaces to achieve better sampling parallels theoretical approaches used in quantum simulation and optimization problems where high barriers limit exploration.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Target one-dimensional potential H(x) (black curve) with the marginal x-histogram and trajectory samples (pink) from the separable HS-REX replica, showing equal occupancy of both minima. (b)–(f) Contours of the two-dimensional hyperspatial potential H(x) and trajectory samples for µ = 100 (separable), 100, 10, 1, and 0.1. As µ decreases, the penalty on the extra coordinate x+ weakens, the accessible region in the extended space expands, and samples at small µ circumnavigate the x-barrier via nonzero x+. Exchange acceptance is ∼100% between the separable replica and µ = 100, and 36–45% between neighboring non-separable pairs. The d = 2 dimensional Hamiltonian is shown in (g).

FIG. 2. Backbone free-energy surfaces ∆F for HS-REX and PT at the physical and enhanced replicas. (a)–(c) show the ability of the methods enhanced replicas to explore the configuration space, (d)–(f) present the sampling under target physical conditions. (a) and (d) are results from HS-REX at (a) µ = 0.5 and (d) the separable system with µ = 2000, respectively. Panels (b) and (e) show the same data, but remapped to L-chiral configurations by transforming D-form frames as (ϕ, ψ) 7→(−ϕ, −ψ). Reference PT simulations are show in (c) for T = 600 K and (f) the target temperature T = 298 K. The data shown uses an identical number of simulation steps. The initial equilibration frames are discarded.

FIG. 3. Signed Cα chirality volume for alanine dipeptide (common trajectory length; first 100 frames discarded). (a) HS-REX physical replica (µ = 2000); gray: PT T = 298 K reference. (b) HS-REX enhanced replica (µ = 0.5) with the same reference.

FIG. 4. Replica-exchange diagnostics for alanine dipeptide (common trajectory length). (a) Per-pair acceptance rates for HS-REX (µ = 2000–0.5, blue) and PT (T = 298–600 K, red); dashed line: optimal 23% [22]. (b) Round-trip time distributions (dashed lines: means).
